title: Why Churchgoers Escaped the ‘Sex Recession’ | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A Gospel Coalition piece on a new IFS report says 62% of religious married couples (attending church at least twice a month) are intimate weekly, compared with 48% of nonreligious couples. The gap opened only in the last 20 years; in the 2000s, religious and secular couples had sex at similar rates.

insights.claim: According to an Institute for Family Studies report, 62% of religious married couples (attending church at least twice a month) are intimate weekly, compared with 48% of nonreligious married couples.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Measures of marital health increasingly differ along religious lines, which matters for forecasts of fertility and household stability.
insights.quote: Sixty-two percent of religious couples are intimate weekly, compared with just 48 percent of nonreligious couples.

insights.claim: In the 2000s, religious and secular US married couples had sex at similar rates, but a large gap has opened over the last 20 years.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The 'sex recession' has hit secular households specifically, which suggests that differences in fertility and family formation between religious and secular Americans are widening.
insights.quote: In the last 20 years, a major gap in sexual activity has opened between religious and secular marriages.

insights.claim: Religious married couples not only have sex more often than secular couples but also report enjoying it more, according to the IFS report.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Higher marital satisfaction among the religious may support more stable unions and more births.
insights.quote: have sex at significantly higher rates than secular married couples and enjoy it more
insights.locator: A new report from the Institute
